what_its_for: Insulin aspart is a fast-acting insulin used to control blood sugar (glucose) levels in people with diabetes (type 1 or type 2). It works like the natural insulin your body makes after eating a meal, helping sugar from food get into your body's cells for energy.
how_to_take: Insulin aspart is given as a shot (injection) under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in your stomach area, thigh, or upper arm. You can also use it in an insulin pump. Always rotate (change) the spot where you inject each time to avoid skin problems. Inject NovoLog/NovoRapid within 5 to 10 minutes BEFORE starting a meal. Inject Fiasp at the START of a meal or within 20 minutes after starting a meal. Never inject into a vein or muscle unless directed by your doctor. Always wash your hands before preparing your dose. Use a new needle each time.
dosing: Your dose is personal and set by your doctor based on your blood sugar levels, diet, activity, and other medications. Do NOT change your dose without talking to your doctor first. Your doctor will tell you exactly how many units to inject and when. Keep a log of your blood sugar readings to help your doctor adjust your dose if needed.
missed_dose: If you forget to take your dose BEFORE a meal, take it as soon as you remember — but only if you are still eating or have just finished eating. If your meal is already done, skip the missed dose and wait for your next scheduled mealtime injection. NEVER double up on doses to make up for a missed one. Check your blood sugar more often if you miss a dose and contact your doctor if you are unsure what to do.
storage: UNOPENED (not yet used) vials, pens, or cartridges: Store in the refrigerator (36°F to 46°F / 2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze. Keep away from the freezer section and ice packs. OPENED (in-use) vials: Can be kept at room temperature (below 86°F / 30°C) for up to 28 days. OPENED (in-use) pens or cartridges: Keep at room temperature (below 86°F / 30°C) for up to 28 days. Do NOT refrigerate opened pens. Keep away from direct sunlight and heat. Throw away any insulin that looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles floating in it — insulin aspart should be clear and colorless. Write the date you opened it on the label so you know when to discard it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid skipping meals after taking your insulin — this can cause dangerously low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Avoid drinking alcohol or limit it greatly, as it can make your blood sugar drop too low or rise unexpectedly. Avoid strenuous exercise right after injecting unless your doctor says it is okay. Avoid changing your insulin brand or type without talking to your doctor first. Do not share your insulin pen, needles, or syringes with anyone else — even family members — as this can spread infections. Avoid driving or using heavy machinery if your blood sugar is low, as it can affect your ability to concentrate and react.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: signs of LOW blood sugar (hypoglycemia) such as shaking, sweating, dizziness, fast heartbeat, confusion, blurred vision, or feeling very hungry — treat low blood sugar immediately with fast-acting sugar (like glucose tablets or juice) and then call your doctor; signs of HIGH blood sugar (hyperglycemia) such as increased thirst, frequent urination, blurry vision, fatigue, or fruity-smelling breath; signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of face/lips/throat, or trouble breathing; redness, swelling, or lumps at your injection site that do not go away; if you are sick, have an infection, or are under unusual stress, as these can change how much insulin you need; if you become pregnant or are planning to become pregnant.
when_it_works: Insulin aspart starts working very quickly — usually within 10 to 20 minutes after injection. It reaches its strongest effect (peak) in about 1 to 3 hours. Its effects last for about 3 to 5 hours. Because it works so fast, it is important to eat your meal shortly after injecting so your blood sugar does not drop too low.
special_populations: PREGNANCY: Insulin is considered safe during pregnancy and is often the preferred treatment for diabetes in pregnant women. Talk to your doctor — your insulin needs may change a lot during pregnancy and after delivery. BREASTFEEDING: Insulin aspart is considered safe while breastfeeding. Your dose may need to be adjusted. ELDERLY (65 years and older): Older adults may be more sensitive to insulin and have a higher risk of low blood sugar. Blood sugar should be monitored closely, and doses may need careful adjustment. CHILDREN: Insulin aspart (NovoLog/NovoRapid) can be used in children as young as 2 years old. Fiasp can be used in children as young as 2 years old as well. Doses are carefully adjusted based on the child's weight and needs. Always follow your child's doctor's instructions closely. KIDNEY or LIVER DISEASE: These conditions can affect how your body processes insulin and may increase your risk of low blood sugar. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose and monitor you more closely.
